title: A hundred years since she was born, twenty-two before anyone can look
material: A room in the house she died in, opened twice a year to check the humidity, with seven canvases in it turned to the wall. A letter in her hand explaining the fifty years, which her niece has never shown anyone. One photograph of her, taken in 1961, which she disliked and which the estate will not release. The humidity log, kept since 1998 in the same biro. Nothing else: the four canvases in institutions cannot be visited and the eleven have never been photographed.
occasion: She was born in 1926 and would have been a hundred on 19 November. Her will directs that no reproduction of any work be made or licensed for fifty years from her death, until 2048. Eleven canvases exist. Nobody under fifty has seen any of them. The centenary arrives and the embargo does not lift, and those two facts have to occupy the same year without either one cancelling the other.
when: The centenary of her birth falls on 19 November. The embargo lifts in 2048, twenty-two years out.
where: The village she worked in for thirty years, which has a hall, a shop and a bus twice a day.
means: One process, whatever a signage and vehicle-livery firm two towns over normally runs, in a fortnight of their October capacity. Their inks, their stock, their machine, set up once. Nothing that needs a second pass and nothing they have to be talked into.
atStake: A promise made to a dying woman by a nineteen-year-old and kept for twenty-six years, with twenty-two still to run. There is no second centenary and the niece is seventy-one. Anything made here that reads as secrecy rather than fidelity starts the pressure to break the embargo now instead of in 2048.
fear: That it becomes an advertisement for something withheld. That would bring exactly the attention the will was written to prevent, and would put seven canvases in a house with one lock on it into the minds of people who had not been thinking about them.
pressures: Everything about the situation pulls towards proving the work was worth the embargo, and the only way to prove that is to describe it, and describing it is the one act the will forbids.

A shape that resembles a composition nobody has seen is still a derivation if anyone argues it is, and the estate cannot afford to find out. The safest surface is one with nothing on it that could be mistaken for hers, which is also the emptiest.

Twenty-six years of being accused of hoarding pull hard towards saying, somewhere on the surface, that this was her instruction and not the family's. Saying so is a defence, and a defence assumes an accusation the work would otherwise not have raised.
The centenary invites commemoration, and commemoration has one register — the dates, the name, the span — which arrives already formed and asks for nothing to be decided.
refusals: No reproduction of any work, in any degree, including a resemblance that could be argued into one. This is not a preference and there is no version of the work that gets to test it.
Not the 1961 photograph. She disliked it, it is the only image of her anywhere, and using it because it is the only one is exactly the reasoning she wrote a will against.
Nothing that makes the seven findable. Not the room, not the house, not the number of locks.
No quotation from the letter. The niece has not said whether it may be quoted, and an unanswered question is not permission.
notes: The niece opens the room in April and October. She has said that she looks at them and that she does not know what she is checking for any more.
